renewal.note: Amazon cancelled Three Pines in March 2023 after one season. Production partners and the streamer reportedly could not reach an agreement on renewal terms despite mutual interest.

bollymeter.basis: Rotten Tomatoes at 72% from 18 critics and Metacritic at 68 from 6 reviews place it in firmly favorable territory; RogerEbert.com called it a collection of intelligent two-hour mysteries for fans of Agatha Christie or Columbo.

pull_quotes.text: A collection of intelligent two-hour mysteries that fans of Agatha Christie or even Columbo should watch.
Handsomely shot snowscapes, a Christmassy setting and Molina's beautifully measured performance make it a moreish winter treat.

seasons.review_body: Three Pines arrived on Prime Video in December 2022 as a prestige adaptation of Louise Penny's beloved Inspector Gamache novels, with Alfred Molina as a casting choice critics consistently praised as the show's strongest asset. The 72 percent Rotten Tomatoes score from 18 reviewers reflected appreciation for the procedural craftsmanship and Molina's measured performance without enthusiasm for the series as a whole. RogerEbert.com called it intelligent Christie-adjacent mysteries. The Telegraph singled out the Quebec snowscapes and Molina's measured work. A running parallel cold case involving a missing Indigenous woman added social weight that critics noted as thoughtful but unevenly integrated. Cancelled after one season despite solid reviews, leaving Penny's expansive book series largely unadapted.

episode_reviews.spoiler_free: Chief Inspector Gamache arrives in Three Pines to investigate a suspicious death while the village's particular rhythms establish the show's cozy-but-unsettling tonal register. Molina's unhurried authority sets the show's pace immediately.

critic_note.text: A quality supporting cast and a light sense of humor helps. Not every aspect of the show is light and airy, but it seems to know when it needs to be serious.

episode_reviews.review_body:
# Three Pines S1E1: "The Hangman - Part 1" Review

*Spoiler-light verdict above. Full episode analysis below.*

The chant comes first. Before the curling rink, before the electrical theory, before the photograph that bends the hour in another direction, the episode opens on a demand for justice now. Then someone says what everyone in power would rather leave buried: no one is dealing with the missing case, and no one ever will.

BollyAI's read: "The Hangman - Part 1" works best when it treats investigation as a fight against delay. Its murder mechanics are clean, its protest frame gives the hour moral pressure, and its late Brooklyn clue opens the season beyond one suspicious death. The weakness is bluntness. The episode sometimes explains the turn before letting the unease breathe.

## The Case Begins Before the Body

The sharpest choice in the premiere is that it does not start with **CC de Poitiers** as a puzzle. It starts with a demand. The repeated call for immediate justice makes the episode's first argument before the detectives can make theirs: procedure is already late. That matters because the next major beat is not a corpse but a missing person case that someone believes has been abandoned.

That line of pressure gives the hour a useful split. On one side, there is the visible death at a public curling match, witnessed by enough people to be initially described as a collapse. On the other, there is the missing case that has already hardened into expectation. No one is handling it. No one will. The episode sets these tracks against each other without pretending they carry the same texture. CC's death gets conventional procedural attention. The missing case gets the moral wound.

That distinction gives the premiere its bite. The murder investigation moves because death happens in public, in front of witnesses, inside a social event. The missing case sits in a different category. It has to be argued back into visibility. That contrast makes the opening protest more than atmosphere. It is a charge against the way attention gets rationed.

The detective confrontation after driving a family home sits neatly inside that structure. It is not a throwaway professional spat. It keeps the premiere's institutional anxiety in motion. What happened that day matters because the episode is already asking whether official attention arrives only when a body falls in public. That is the stronger engine here. A corpse can start a case. Neglect starts a reckoning.

The hour does not yet resolve that tension, and it should not. This is Part 1. What matters is that the missing case is not treated as background color for a murder mystery. It presses against the main plot from the start, turning the investigation into a test of priorities as much as evidence.

## A Curling Match Becomes a Crime Scene

The first account of CC's death is deliberately ordinary in its phrasing. She was watching a curling match, then she collapsed. The mundanity is the trap. A community event, a public setting, a sudden fall. At that stage, the hour can still wear the shape of a freak accident.

Then the walkthrough tightens. The episode links the location to an old residential school for Indigenous kids, which gives the setting an ugly historical charge before the forensics have finished doing their work. That link is one of the hour's better structural moves. It refuses to let the murder sit as a sealed-off whodunit object. Place has memory here, and the premiere makes the murder location carry more than logistics.

The risk is that the episode is carrying two weights at once: a technical murder method and a larger history of institutional damage. The technical side is more immediately legible. The residential school reference arrives with force, but the dossier's beats show it functioning as a location link more than a fully dramatized thread in this part. That does not make it hollow. It does mean the hour is planting a heavier idea than it can fully harvest in Part 1.

Still, as a first-episode move, it is smart. The case is not staged in neutral space. Even when the investigation is talking about puddles, power, and timing, the ground underneath has already been marked.

The curling rink also helps the mystery because it gives the episode a public crime with private intent. The killer has to work inside a shared space, exploiting the ordinary layout of a room that no one is treating as dangerous. That tension matters. The more normal the setting looks, the nastier the design becomes once the mechanics click into place.

## The Electric Chair Detail Does the Heavy Lifting

The forensics sequence is the premiere at its most confident. Washer fluid puddle. Bare hands and boots. An electrified source. The explanation moves the death from accident to design, and the clean horror of it is that CC's seat becomes the murder weapon. A public place has been converted into a trap.

This is the hour's strongest procedural beat because it makes the murder method visual. The audience does not need a lecture about voltage when the construction is this plain: liquid placed where it should not be, exposed skin, a path for current, a victim sitting in the wrong seat. The method has the nasty elegance of a good mystery device. It is theatrical, but it is still built from ordinary objects.

That matters for a village mystery. The best version of this mode turns familiar spaces hostile without making them feel absurd. "The Hangman - Part 1" gets that balance right in the electrocution reveal. The explanation is heightened, but it is not untethered. It asks the viewer to re-evaluate the room rather than accept a random contrivance.

BollyAI's criticism lands here too. The episode moves quickly from possible accident to increasingly confident intentional setup. That serves momentum, but it shaves off some paranoia. A staged electrocution should create a little more uncertainty before the theory locks in. The dossier's central contradiction points to that exact pressure: earlier treatment as a freak collapse, then a rapid march toward deliberate murder.

That speed is not fatal. It does, however, make the investigation feel more efficient than unsettling. The episode knows where it is going, and sometimes it lets the audience feel the outline before the dread has time to settle. A little more hesitation around the mechanics would have made the reveal hit harder.

Even so, the electric-chair image is effective because it condenses the case into one brutal idea. The killer did not merely strike CC. The killer used the room against her.

## The Brooklyn Photograph Opens the Other Door

The late photograph taken two weeks earlier in a Brooklyn housing project gives the premiere its best reversal. The missing case is no longer only an accusation of official failure. It becomes active evidence. **Blue Two-Rivers** may be alive, and that possibility changes the emotional temperature of the hour.

This is where the episode's structure pays off. Because the premiere began with protest and despair, the Brooklyn clue does not feel like a random cliffhanger. It answers the opening mood with movement. The missing case had been framed by absence and neglect. The photograph introduces presence. Someone existed recently enough to be caught by a camera, far from the assumptions surrounding the case.

The timing is good. By placing this after the forensic clarification around CC's death, the episode avoids becoming a single-track murder puzzle. It says the season's attention will be divided between the death everyone can see and the disappearance some fear has already been written off. That gives the first chapter a broader shape than a standard village-murder opener.

The clue also reframes the protest without softening it. If Blue may be alive, the anger at the start does not become mistaken. It becomes urgent in a different way. The failure is not only that people stopped looking. It is that the case may still be moving while the system has already decided it is over.

The final sudden note that CC de Poitiers is no longer there adds another jolt, though it is less clean in isolation than the photograph. As a cliff-edge beat, it works because the hour has already made CC's death suspicious, public, and mechanically strange. As a piece of clarity, it withholds more than it gives. That is acceptable for Part 1, but the next chapter has to cash the confusion, not simply extend it.

That is the challenge the premiere hands to the season. The show has opened two doors: one forensic, one institutional. The Brooklyn photograph is the more promising of the two because it widens the story without loosening it. It gives the episode momentum past the autopsy board and into a larger question of who gets searched for, who gets believed, and who gets left behind.

## The Verdict

"The Hangman - Part 1" is a sturdy, pointed opener with one excellent murder mechanism and a sharper second case pushing underneath it. Its best instinct is to make justice a timing problem: the chant wants it now, the missing case has waited too long, and the murder investigation becomes urgent once CC drops in public. The episode's weaker instinct is over-explanation. It sometimes states the shape of the crime before the dread has settled.

BollyAI's read: this is solid mystery construction with a moral frame strong enough to keep the mechanics from feeling decorative. The season begins with two engines, one forensic and one institutional, and the Brooklyn photograph is the beat that gives the larger arc its pulse.

verdict.one_liner: A sharp procedural opener where the murder method clicks, though the hour explains its suspicion a shade too quickly.
